title: Space industry of India
wikitext:
{{Short description|Overview of Indian space sector}} {{Use Indian English|date=February 2021}} {{Use dmy dates|date=February 2021}} The '''space industry of India''' is predominantly driven by its national space agency [[ISRO]]. The industry includes over 500 private suppliers and other various bodies of the [[Department of Space]] (DoS) in all commercial, research and arbitrary regards. Since the Indian space sector was opened up to [[private sector]] in 2020, numerous private space companies have emerged, working on various aspects of [[space exploration]]. In 2023, the space industry of India accounted for US$9 billion or 2%–3% of the [[Space industry|global space industry]] and employed more than 45,000 people. The [[Government of India]] projects industry to grow four to five times over the next 8–10 years, potentially reaching US$40–45 billion, global share targeted to rise to 8% by 2030.{{cite web|date=21 June 2026 |title = India’s space economy projected to reach $40–45 billion over next decade |url = https://www.thehansindia.com/tech/indias-space-economy-projected-to-reach-4045-billion-over-next-decade-1088762 |access-date=27 July 2026|work=The Hans India}} [[File:PSLV C45 EMISAT campaign 09.jpg|right|thumb|290px|Integration of [[Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle]] underway]] As of 2025, India has launched [[List of foreign satellites launched by India|434 satellites]] for various foreign countries. There were more than 300 space startups in India in mid 2025 involved in various stages of developing their own [[Launch vehicle|launch vehicles]], designing satellites and other allied activities.{{Cite news |title='Bharat aaj bhi saare jahan se acha dikhta hai': Astronaut Shubhanshu Shukla recounts space journey; talks about Axiom-4 mission |url=https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/india/bharat-aaj-bhi-saare-jahan-se-acha-dikhta-hai-astronaut-shubhanshu-shukla-recounts-space-journey-talks-about-axiom-4-mission/articleshow/123427229.cms |access-date=2025-08-21 |work=The Times of India |issn=0971-8257}} By 2026, the industry had expanded to almost 400 start ups and over 500 public limited and state-owned companies.{{citation needed|date=July 2026}} == History == === Early decades === India's interest in space travel began in the early 1960s, when scientists launched a [[Nike-Apache]] rocket from [[Thumba Equatorial Rocket Launching Station]] (TERLS), [[Thiruvananthapuram]].{{cite news| title = The dawn of a new space race?| url = https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/asia-pacific/4208176.stm | work=BBC News | date=2005-10-14 | access-date=2010-01-01}}{{Cite news|url=http://www.thebetterindia.com/74283/first-rocket-india-thumba-vikram-sarabhai-abdul-kalam/|title=Transported on a Bicycle, Launched from a Church: The Amazing Story of India's First Rocket Launch|date=2016-11-08|work=The Better India|access-date=2017-07-04|language=en-US}} The [[Indian National Committee for Space Research]] was subsequently set up, which later became ISRO functioning under a new independent DoS in the 1970s under the [[Prime Minister of India]].{{Cite web |url=https://www.isro.gov.in/about-isro/department-of-space-and-isro-hq |title=Department of Space and ISRO HQ - ISRO |access-date=19 February 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190328053630/https://www.isro.gov.in/about-isro/department-of-space-and-isro-hq |archive-date=28 March 2019 |url-status=live }}{{sfn|Sadeh|2013|pp=303}} ISRO joined the [[Interkosmos]] program to launch its first satellite, [[Aryabhata (satellite)|Aryabhata]], from the former Soviet Union in 1975.{{cite web|url=https://www.isro.gov.in/Spacecraft/aryabhata-1|title=Aryabhata – ISRO|website=www.isro.gov.in|access-date=19 February 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180815200808/https://www.isro.gov.in/Spacecraft/aryabhata-1|archive-date=15 August 2018|url-status=live}} [[Satellite Launch Vehicle|SLV-3]], a locally developed space rocket, was introduced in 1979, enabling India to undertake orbital launches.{{cite web|url=https://www.isro.gov.in/sites/default/files/flipping_book/58-SI-Jul-Sep-05/files/assets/common/downloads/publication.pdf|title=First Successful Launch of SLV-3 - Silver Jubilee|publisher=ISRO|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220523115130/https://www.isro.gov.in/sites/default/files/flipping_book/58-SI-Jul-Sep-05/files/assets/common/downloads/publication.pdf|archive-date=23 May 2022}} Experience gained from SLV-3 was used to develop ASLV to develop technologies for launching satellites in [[geostationary orbit]], but this ended up having very limited success and was eventually discontinued.{{cite news|last=Menon|first=Amarnath|title=Setback in the sky|url=https://www.indiatoday.in/magazine/science-and-technology/story/19870415-failure-of-aslv-mission-comes-a-major-blow-to-india-ambitious-space-programme-798754-1987-04-14|access-date=19 February 2021|newspaper=India Today|date=15 April 1987}} However, the study of a homegrown [[medium-lift launch vehicle]] went on, which lead to the realisation of the PSLV.{{cite news|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=IbbMj56ht8sC&pg=PA215|title=Indian ambitions in space go sky-high|date=22 January 1981|publisher=New Scientist|page=215}} The Government of India forayed into space exploration when scientists started to launch [[sounding rockets]] from TERLS. The establishment of the space agency lead to the development of small launch vehicles SLV-3 and [[Augmented Satellite Launch Vehicle|ASLV]], followed by larger [[Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle|PSLV]] and [[Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle|GSLV]] rockets in the 1990s, which allowed India to shift larger payloads and undertake commercial launches for the international market. Private firms started to emerge later as subcontractors for various rocket and [[satellite]] components. Reforms liberalising the space sector and nondisclosure agreements came in the late 2010s, leading to the emergence of various private spaceflight companies. === Introduction of PSLV and commercial space missions === [[Antrix Corporation]] was set up in 1992 to market ISRO's technology, launch services and transfer technology to Indian private firms, dawning the commercial space sector in India.{{cite web|url=https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/india/Antrix-responsible-for-marketing-ISRO-tech/articleshow/7457366.cms|archive-url=https://archive.today/20130426170804/http://articles.timesofindia.indiatimes.com/2011-02-09/india/28547101_1_isro-eads-astrium-antrix-corporation|url-status=live|archive-date=26 April 2013|work=[[The Times of India]]|title=Antrix responsible for marketing ISRO tech|date=9 February 2011 |access-date=21 February 2021}} The PSLV rocket, introduced in 1993, enabled India to launch its polar satellites. Despite initial failures in its first two flights, PSLV had no further failures and emerged as ISRO's primary workhorse for launching domestic and foreign satellites.{{cite web|title=India (Launchers)|url=http://claudelafleur.qc.ca/Indians-launchers.html|publisher=Spacecraft Encyclopedia|access-date=12 November 2014}}{{cite web|title=PSLV|url=http://space.skyrocket.de/doc_lau/pslv.htm|website=Gunter's Space Page|access-date=12 November 2014}} The development of GSLV and [[LVM3]] subsequently began in the 1990s and 2000s to attain the capability to launch [[communication satellites]]. However, the launchers didn't become operational until decades later, as India initially faced a great problem in the development of [[cryogenic engine]]s.{{cite journal|title=GSLV Launched Successfully| journal=Current Science|date=May 2001| volume=80| issue=10| page=1256| url=http://www.iisc.ernet.in/currsci/may252001/1254.pdf| access-date=12 December 2013}}{{cite news| last=Subramanian| first=T S| title=The GSLV Quest| url=http://www.frontline.in/navigation/?type=static&page=flonnet&rdurl=fl1806/18060820.htm |access-date=21 February 2021| newspaper=Frontline| date=March 17–31, 2001}}{{Cite web|url = http://www.sawfnews.com/Health/70695.aspx|title = India's GSLV Mk-3 First Flight Pushed Back to April 2014|date = 4 April 2013|access-date = 21 February 2021|website = Sawfnews|url-status = usurped|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20130410172341/http://www.sawfnews.com/Health/70695.aspx|archive-date = 10 April 2013}} Later, [[NewSpace India Limited]] (NSIL) replaced Antrix Corporation as the commercial arm of ISRO.{{cite news|title=New Company for Commercial Exploitation of Research and Development (Under The Company Act 2013) |url=https://pib.gov.in/PressReleaseIframePage.aspx?PRID=1576000|newspaper=Press Information Bureau|access-date=3 March 2021|date=27 June 2019}} === Mission DefSpace === The Defence Innovation Organisation (DIO), through its Innovations for Defence Excellence (iDEX) framework, has become a key catalyst in advancing India's indigenous defence and space innovation landscape.[https://www.idex.gov.in/about-us About iDEX – Defence Innovation Organisation] By bridging the gap between defence user requirements and private-sector innovation, DIO promotes dual-use technological development that supports both strategic and commercial applications.[https://pib.gov.in/PressReleaseIframePage.aspx?PRID=1870456 PIB: Mission DefSpace announcement and objectives] The launch of Mission DefSpace in October 2022 marked a significant milestone—uniting startups, MSMEs, and academia to co-develop solutions in satellite communication, Earth observation, Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR), AI-driven geospatial analytics, and space situational awareness (SSA).[https://www.mod.gov.in/dod/idex-defence-innovation-organisation MoD: DIO – iDEX Overview][https://www.hindustantimes.com/india-news/pm-launches-75-defence-challenges-including-3-under-defspace-initiative-101666821424824.html Hindustan Times: PM launches 75 iDEX challenges including DefSpace] With challenge-based funding, technology mentorship, and procurement-linked incentives, DIO's role has been instrumental in nurturing a sustainable ecosystem for India's growing space-defence industry.[https://www.financialexpress.com/defence/mission-defspace-an-initiative-to-boost-indias-space-defence-capabilities/2764440/ Financial Express: Mission DefSpace – boosting India's space-defence capabilities] Under the Mission DefSpace, several companies have signed agreements with DIO/iDEX to develop technologies critical for India's military and strategic space applications.[https://www.business-standard.com/india-news/idex-under-dio-signs-first-defspace-challenges-contracts-with-startups-124022900695_1.html Business Standard: iDEX under DIO signs DefSpace agreements with startups] For instance, Sisir Radar Pvt. Ltd., founded by former ISRO Director Tapan Misra, is developing an L- and P-band continuous-wave Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) payload along with an unfurlable, electronically steered antenna for small-satellite platforms—enhancing India's all-weather imaging and reconnaissance capabilities.[https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/india/former-isro-directors-startup-wins-idex-challenge-for-developing-sar-payload-for-satellites/articleshow/104568003.cms Times of India: Former ISRO Director's startup wins iDEX challenge] Similarly, Space Kidz India has taken up the challenge of designing CubeSat deployers for microgravity and small-satellite missions, supporting low-cost and rapid satellite deployment for defence and scientific applications.[https://www.careerindia.com/news/enhancing-cubesat-separation-technology-011-048111.html Career India: Enhancing CubeSat Separation Technology][https://www.moneycontrol.com/news/business/isro-to-launch-space-kidz-india-satellite-made-by-750-school-children-9818131.html Moneycontrol: ISRO to launch Space Kidz India satellite] Kepler Aerospace Pvt. Ltd., another participant, is working on CubeSat-class satellite platforms designed for real-time surveillance and communication relays, demonstrating the diversity of innovation emerging through the DefSpace initiative.[https://www.rediff.com/news/report/kepler-wins-defence-deal-for-swarming-satellites/20250709.htm Rediff: Kepler wins Defence Deal for Swarming Satellites][https://www.indiandefensenews.in/2025/07/kepler-secures-4-million-idex-prime.html Indian Defence News: Kepler secures $4 million iDEX Prime contract] Alongside these, firms such as Digantara, Antsys Innovations, SpacePixxel, GalaxEye Space, and InspeCity Space Laboratories are contributing across domains including space domain awareness, RF communications, and on-orbit servicing—collectively reinforcing India's goal of achieving self-reliance and strategic depth in space-defence technologies.[https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/industry/defence/mission-defspace-aims-to-strengthen-indias-space-defence-capabilities-idex/articleshow/95068772.cms Economic Times: Mission DefSpace aims to strengthen India's space-defence capabilities][https://pib.gov.in/PressReleaseIframePage.aspx?PRID=1925638 PIB: iDEX DefSpace programme update, 2024] === Emergence of the private sector === {{Main|Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre|Space Activities Bill}} The Indian space programme emerged as an economic sector with government-backed investments with official institutions in the military and civilian administrations over decades of engineering. Over four decades, ISRO continued transferring technologies to [[small and medium enterprises]] (SMEs), leading to there being over 500 suppliers of various components in 2017.{{sfn|Rajagopalan|Prasad|2017|pp=1-2}} [[Information technology in India|India's IT industry]] started engaging in this sector in the 1990s. The Department of Space actively promoted the growth of the sector, leading to the establishment of the manufacturing of various systems. Large mapping projects for various civilian and military requirements were outsourced by the government, which drove the growth of India's private space sector. However, the private sector still played a supporting role, while the government continued to dominate the space sector.{{sfn|Rajagopalan|Prasad|2017|pp=54}} In the late 2010s, a large number of startups started to emerge throughout the country with their own proposals and concepts to develop various satellite technologies and rockets.{{Cite news|last=Singh|first=Abhinav|date=2017-07-02|title=Space no bar|url=https://www.theweek.in/theweek/business/indias-young-space-entrepreneurs.html|newspaper=The Week|access-date=2021-03-04}}{{Cite news|last1=Ravikumar|first1=Sachin|last2=Shakil|first2=Ismail|date=2019-06-23|title=India's space startups ignite investor interest|url=https://www.livemint.com/news/india/india-s-space-startups-ignite-investor-interest-1561269988291.html|newspaper=LiveMint|via=Reuters|access-date=2021-03-04}}{{Cite news|last=Arakali|first=Harichandan|date=2019-09-09|title=Space-tech startups in India are gaining ground|url=https://www.forbesindia.com/article/startups/spacetech-startups-in-india-are-gaining-ground/55181/1|newspaper=Forbes India|access-date=2021-03-04}} A range of initiatives to deregulate the private space sector were introduced by [[Narendra Modi]]'s cabinet in June 2020, and the [[Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre]] (IN-SPACe) was established for incubating technology into private firms, known as Non-Government Private Entities (NGPEs) by DOS.{{Cite news|date=2020-06-26|title=India opens space sector to private players: What it means for ISRO|url=https://www.financialexpress.com/lifestyle/science/india-opens-space-sector-to-private-players-what-it-means-for-isro/2005105/|newspaper=Financial Express|access-date=2021-03-04}}a) {{Cite web|title='UNLOCKING INDIA'S POTENTIAL IN SPACE SECTOR'|url=https://www.isro.gov.in/unlocking-india%E2%80%99s-potential-space-sector}};
b) {{Cite web|title=Emerging trend in Space Sector|url=https://www.isro.gov.in/unlocking-india%E2%80%99s-potential-space-sector/emerging-trend-space-sector}};
c) {{Cite web|title=Opening Up Indian Space Sector For Private Sector –Reforms|url=https://www.isro.gov.in/unlocking-india%E2%80%99s-potential-space-sector/opening-indian-space-sector-private-sector-%E2%80%93reforms}};
d) {{Cite web|title=Space Activities By NGPEs|url=https://www.isro.gov.in/unlocking-india%E2%80%99s-potential-space-sector/space-activities-ngpes}};
e) {{Cite web|title=Enabling Mechanism For NGPEs To Carry Out Space Activities|url=https://www.isro.gov.in/unlocking-india%E2%80%99s-potential-space-sector/enabling-mechanism-ngpes-to-carry-out-space-activities}};
Indian Space Research Organisation - Government of India. Retrieved on 4 March 2021. NGPEs were included as a crucial part of ISRO's Space Communication Policy draft issued in October 2020.{{Cite report|date=2020-10-15|title=No.C.19013/48/2012-Sec.3 (Vol.III) Spacecom Policy - 2020 and Spacecom NGP-2020|url=https://www.isro.gov.in/sites/default/files/draft_spacecom_policy_2020.pdf|publisher=Department of Space |page= |docket= |access-date=2021-03-04|quote=}} As of 2021, a new [[Space Activities Bill]] and a space policy are being drafted by [[NALSAR University of Law|NALSAR Centre for Aerospace and Defence laws]] to regulate space manufacturing and the legal aspects of the industry in India.{{Cite news|date=2020-07-05|title=Space policy, Space Activities Bill in final stages: ISRO chairman|url=https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/news/science/space-policy-space-activities-bill-in-final-stages-isro-chairman/articleshow/76800775.cms|newspaper=The Economic Times|access-date=2021-03-04}}{{Cite interview |last=Reddy|first=V Balakista |subject-link= |interviewer=Preeti Biswas|title='Space Activities Bill reflects years of research … it will bring clarity and synergy to both Indian and foreign companies' |url=https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/blogs/the-interviews-blog/space-activities-bill-reflects-years-of-research-it-will-bring-clarity-and-synergy-to-both-indian-and-foreign-companies/ |publisher= |location= |date=2020-09-30|work=The Times of India |access-date=2021-03-04}} In 2021, the Government of India launched the [[Indian Space Association]] (ISpA) to open the Indian space industry to private sectors and start-ups. Several private companies like [[Larsen & Toubro]], Nelco ([[Tata Group]]), [[Eutelsat OneWeb|OneWeb]], [[MapmyIndia]], [[Walchandnagar Industries]] are founding members of this organisation.{{cite news |title=PM Modi launches Indian Space Association for govt, pvt coordination |url=https://indianexpress.com/article/technology/science/pm-modi-launches-indian-space-association-for-govt-pvt-coordination-7566992/ |access-date=22 November 2021 |publisher=The Indian Express |date=12 October 2021}} Lieutenant General [[Anil Kumar Bhatt]] was appointed as the Director General of ISpA.{{cite news |title=Space sector to become engine of growth for economy: ISpA's DG |url=https://telecom.economictimes.indiatimes.com/news/space-sector-to-become-engine-of-growth-for-economy-ispas-dg/86930937 |access-date=22 November 2021 |publisher=The Economic Times |date=11 October 2021}} An amendment was made in the FDI policy for space sector through a gazette notification dated 16 April 2024, called the Foreign Exchange Management (Non-debt Instruments) (Third Amendment) Rules, 2024. The liberalized entry routes under the amended policy are aimed at attracting potential investors in the Indian companies in space. As per them, up to 74% FDI for satellite manufacturing & operation, satellite data products and ground segment & user segment are allowed under automatic route. Beyond 74% these activities are under government route. FDI up to 49% is allowed for launch vehicles and associated systems or subsystems, creation of spaceports for launching and receiving spacecraft are under automatic route but beyond 49% government permission would be required. The cabinet on 21 February had allowed 74% foreign direct investment (FDI) under automatic route for satellite manufacturing, up to 49% under automatic route for launch vehicles, and up to 100% under automatic route for manufacturing of components and systems. The new rules will come into effect from 16 April 2024.{{Cite web |title=Centre Notifies New FDI Rules For Space Sector Ahead Of Elon Musk's Visit |url=https://www.ndtv.com/business-news/centre-notifies-new-fdi-rules-for-space-sector-ahead-of-elon-musks-visit-5463497 |access-date=2024-04-17 |website=NDTV.com}}{{Cite web |title=Space FDI: Finance ministry notifies FDI in space sector; gives better access to capital, say startups |url=https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/tech/startups/finance-ministry-notifies-fdi-in-space-sector-gives-better-access-to-capital-say-startups/articleshow/109381193.cms |access-date=2024-04-17 |website=[[The Economic Times]] |date=17 April 2024 }}{{Cite web |last=Sinha |first=Shishir |date=2024-04-17 |title=Finance Ministry notifies new FDI limits for satellite-related activities under FEMA |url=https://www.thehindubusinessline.com/news/science/finance-ministry-notifies-new-fdi-limits-for-satellite-related-activities-under-fema/article68074526.ece |access-date=2024-04-17 |website=BusinessLine |language=en}} Throughout this time, various nondisclosure agreements and tech transfers have been taking place between ISRO and private entities.{{cite web|url=https://www.newsbharati.com/Encyc/2021/2/12/-ISRO.amp.html|title=In a first of ISRO's history, it tests its first private satellite|date=12 February 2021|publisher=News Bharati}}{{Cite news|date=2020-12-03|title=Non-Disclosure Agreement signed with M/s Agnikul|url=https://www.isro.gov.in/update/03-dec-2020/non-disclosure-agreement-signed-with-m-s-agnikul|work=ISRO - Government of India|access-date=2021-03-04}} In July 2024, Minister of Finance [[Nirmala Sitharaman]] announced that the Indian government will form a US$119 million venture capital find for space startups in India.{{Cite web |last= |date=23 July 2024 |title=India unveils 10 bln rupee venture capital fund for space sector |url=https://www.reuters.com/technology/space/india-unveils-10-bln-rupee-venture-capital-fund-space-sector-2024-07-23/ |access-date=23 October 2024 |website=Reuters}} The [[Union Council of Ministers|Union Cabinet of India]] approved the creation of the venture capital fund in October 2024.{{Cite web |last=India Today Science Desk |date=2024-10-25 |title=Space industry welcomes Cabinet approval of Rs 1,000 crore venture fund |url=https://www.indiatoday.in/science/story/space-industry-welcomes-cabinet-approval-of-rs-1000-crore-venture-fund-2623177-2024-10-25 |access-date=2024-10-28 |website=India Today |language=en}} India has more than 400 private space enterprises as of 2024, up from 54 in 2020. Since 2025, an increasing number of private sector Indian space companies have been setting up offices and forming subsidiaries in the United States to gain access to the American market and compete with domestic U.S. space companies. Some Indian companies, including [[Bellatrix Aerospace]], a satellite propulsion manufacturer, are establishing manufacturing facilities in the U.S.{{Cite news |date=19 May 2025 |title=Indian space-tech startups set offices, mfg facilities in US |url=https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/business/india-business/indian-space-tech-startups-set-offices-mfg-facilities-in-us/articleshow/121274623.cms |access-date=21 May 2025 |work=The Times of India |issn=0971-8257}} As of May 2025, India is planning to launch 52 [[Reconnaissance satellite|spy satellites]] over the next five years, with private sector companies building half of the 52 spy satellites, with ISRO manufacturing the remaining half.{{Cite news |date=2025-05-07 |title=India to launch 52 spy satellites over next five years: INSPACe chairman |url=https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/news/science/india-to-launch-52-spy-satellites-over-next-five-years-inspace-chairman/articleshow/120969293.cms?from=mdr |access-date=2025-05-21 |work=The Economic Times |issn=0013-0389}} Additionally as of May 2025, technology for ISRO's [[Small Satellite Launch Vehicle|SSLV]] is in the process of being [[Technology transfer|transferred]] to private firms by ISRO. On 18 July 2026, the launch of [[Vikram-1]] was successful, with mission meeting all it's objectives and deploying payload at an altitude of {{cvt|453|km|mi}}. [[Skyroot Aerospace]] became the first private Indian company to successfully reach the space in first attempt. This made India the third country in world after the U.S. and China to have rocket launch by private company.{{Cite web |title=Vikram-1: India's first private space rocket by Skyroot to carry diamond flower|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/clyekv7rld3o|date=2026-07-18|access-date=2026-07-18|website=www.bbc.com|language=en-GB}} == Industry overview == ISRO and DoS continue to remain dominant in the national space sector, having launched more than 100 domestic and more than 300 foreign satellites for 33 countries,{{cite news|url=https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/india/isro-milestone-300-satellites-from-33-nations-put-in-space-in-20-years/articleshow/72268186.cms|title=Isro milestone: 300 satellites from 33 nations put in space in 20 years|publisher=Times of India|date=28 November 2019}} while private firms have gradually been gaining ground.{{sfn|Pardoe|1987|pp=14}}{{sfn|Sadeh|2013|pp=303-}}{{Cite web|url=https://www.researchandmarkets.com/reports/5146359/evolving-indian-space-ecosystem-attracting-new|title=Evolving Indian Space Ecosystem Attracting New Space Participants in the Industry, 2020|first=Research and Markets|last=ltd|website=www.researchandmarkets.com}} In 2019, the space industry of India accounted for US$7 billion or 2% of the global space industry and employed more than 45,000 people.{{Cite news|url=https://www.business-standard.com/article/companies/india-s-aerospace-start-ups-eye-rocket-launches-and-planetary-missions-120062601687_1.html|title=India's aerospace start-ups eye rocket launches and planetary missions|first=Peerzada Abrar Samreen Ahmad & Gireesh|last=Babu|newspaper=Business Standard India|date=June 26, 2020|via=Business Standard}} Antrix Corporation expects the industry to grow up to US$50 billion by 2024 if provided with appropriate policy support.{{Cite news|last=Narasimhan|first=TE|date=2020-01-31|title=Space sector can hit $50 bn by 2024, needs policy support: Antrix-PwC study|url=https://wap.business-standard.com/budget/article-amp/space-sector-can-hit-50-bn-by-2024-needs-policy-support-antrix-pwc-study-120013101493_1.html|newspaper=[[Business Standard]]|access-date=2021-02-18}} In February 2020, there were 35 startups that came up in the space sector, of which three focused on designing rockets, 14 on designing satellites, and the rest on drone-based applications and services sector. The number further grew to over 40 in January 2021.{{cite news|url=https://www.hindustantimes.com/education/startups-to-play-key-role-in-indian-space-industry/story-UI0VNbXOivXicQRicvIhgO.html|title='Startups to play key role in Indian space industry'|date= 28 February 2020|publisher=[[Hindustan Times]]}}{{cite news|url=https://www.deccanherald.com/national/india-lagging-behind-us-china-in-space-sector-over-40-start-ups-working-with-govt-economic-survey-945053.html|title=India lagging behind US, China in space sector; over 40 start-ups working with govt: Economic Survey|date=29 January 2021|publisher=[[Deccan Herald]]}} Two companies, Skyroot Aerospace and [[AgniKul Cosmos]] have launched their own [[sounding rocket]]. Skyroot is planning the first launch of its Vikram-1 rocket in 2026, while AgniKul Cosmos is in advanced stages of developing its [[Agnibaan]] launch vehicle.{{Cite news|date=2020-12-28|title=Skyroot tests solid propulsion rocket engine, aims at a rocket by 2021 end|url=https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/tech/startups/skyroot-tests-solid-propulsion-rocket-engine-aims-at-a-rocket-by-2021-end/articleshow/79991647.cms|newspaper=The Economic Times|access-date=2021-03-04}}{{Cite news|date=2021-02-11|title=Agnikul Cosmos fires single-piece, 3D printed rocket engine|url=https://www.moneycontrol.com/news/business/agnikul-cosmos-fires-single-piece-3d-printed-rocket-engine-6491661.html|newspaper=MoneyControl|access-date=2021-03-04}} The space industry has contributed US$60 billion to India's [[gross domestic product]] (GDP) between 2014 and 2024. It created 96,000 direct jobs and 4.7 million indirect jobs, according to the Socio-Economic Impact Analysis of Indian Space Programme Report. India now has the eighth-largest space economy in the world, with space sector earnings reaching US$6.3 billion as of 2023.{{Cite news |last=Singh |first=Surendra |date=2024-11-14 |title=For every rupee Isro spends, return is Rs 2.5, says space agency chief |url=https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/india/for-every-rupee-isro-spends-return-is-rs-2-5-says-space-agency-chief/articleshow/115273716.cms |access-date=2024-12-03 |work=The Times of India |issn=0971-8257}}{{Cite news |last=Koshy |first=Jacob |date=2024-08-23 |title='Space sector contributed ₹20,000 crore to India's GDP over the last decade' |url=https://www.thehindu.com/sci-tech/science/space-sector-contributed-20000-crore-to-indias-gdp-over-the-last-decade/article68559540.ece |url-access=subscription |access-date=2024-10-10 |work=The Hindu |language=en-IN |issn=0971-751X}}The Indian economy has benefited from a multiplier effect of US$2.54 for every dollar earned by the Indian space industry according to the European consulting firm Novaspace, with India's space industry workforce being 2.5 times more productive than the country's wider industrial workforce. At a [[compound annual growth rate]] (CAGR) of 6%, the Indian space economy which is valued at approximately [[₹]]81,050.63 crore (US$8.4 billion) as of 2024 is projected to reach US$13 billion by 2025, accounting for 2% to 3% of the worldwide space economy. The entire amount of money invested in ISRO over the past 55 years since its founding is less than NASA's annual budget. Compared to [[CNSA]], which receives over US$18 billion, and [[NASA]], which works with a budget surpassing $25 billion, ISRO's annual budget in 2024 is approximately US$1.6 billion.{{Cite web |last=Singh |first=Srijan Pal |date=2024-11-06 |title=Why Isro's low-budget hangover is not sustainable for India's future plans |url=https://www.indiatoday.in/science/story/why-isros-low-budget-hangover-is-not-sustainable-for-indias-future-plans-2628271-2024-11-06 |access-date=2024-12-03 |website=India Today |language=en}}{{Cite web |last=Wall |first=Mike |date=2024-03-11 |title=NASA gets $25.4 billion in White House's 2025 budget request |url=https://www.space.com/nasa-white-house-2025-budget-request |access-date=2024-12-03 |website=Space.com |language=en}} India's space industry aims to focus on various niches in the space domain, which include retrieving space data, constructing small satellites and cheap launches into orbit.{{Cite web |last=Bhattacharjee |first=Nivedita |date=14 October 2024 |title=India's space strategy: harness data and tiny satellites to capture market beyond SpaceX |url=https://www.reuters.com/technology/space/indias-space-strategy-harness-data-tiny-satellites-capture-market-beyond-spacex-2024-10-14/ |access-date=23 October 2024 |website=Reuters}} == List of notable organisations and companies == === Major organisations and conglomerates === {| class="wikitable sortable" style="text-align:left" |- ! The space industry of India is predominantly driven by its national space agency ISRO. The industry includes over 500 private suppliers and other various bodies of the Department of Space (DoS) in all commercial, research and arbitrary regards. Since the Indian space sector was opened up to private sector in 2020, numerous private space companies have emerged, working on various aspects of space exploration. In 2023, the space industry of India accounted for US$9 billion or 2%–3% of the global space industry and employed more than 45,000 people. The Government of India projects industry to grow four to five times over the next 8–10 years, potentially reaching US$40–45 billion, global share targeted to rise to 8% by 2030.

As of 2025, India has launched 434 satellites for various foreign countries. There were more than 300 space startups in India in mid 2025 involved in various stages of developing their own launch vehicles, designing satellites and other allied activities. By 2026, the industry had expanded to almost 400 start ups and over 500 public limited and state-owned companies.
